```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  message  = FALSE,
  warning  = FALSE,
  fig.width  = 10,
  fig.height = 7,
  dpi = 90
)
```

A common HTNA question is whether the same actor partition behaves
*differently* across cohorts -- e.g. early-phase versus late-phase
sessions of an interaction corpus; control vs. experimental groups; 
female vs. male, etc. `build_htna()` supports this
directly by passing the session-level grouping column to the function. 
The result is  **one network per cohort**, each preserving the actor partition.
Every other function in `htna` recognises the grouped result and
iterates over cohorts.

## An early / late example

We use the bundled `human_ai` corpus (Human + AI codes from
`Nestimate::human_long` / `ai_long`, with a slightly simplified
alphabet -- see `?human_ai`). Sessions are split chronologically:
ordered by their first `session_date` (with `session_id` as a
deterministic tiebreak), the first half of the sessions form the
*Early* cohort and the rest form the *Late* cohort, reflected 
in the `phase` column. The count below is the number of coded events
(rows) in each cohort:

```{r}
library(htna)
data(human_ai)
xtabs(~ phase, data = human_ai)
```

## Building one network per cohort

`build_htna()` takes the long data frame, the actor-type column, and a
`group` argument naming the session-level cohort column:

```{r}
grp <- build_htna(
  human_ai,
  actor_type = "actor_type",
  group      = "phase"
)
names(grp)
```

The result is a named list of HTNA networks of class `htna_group`, one
per cohort. `summary()` describes every cohort in turn: its actor
partition, how the non-zero edges distribute across the actor blocks,
and the network-level metrics.

```{r}
summary(grp)
```

Because both cohorts were built from the same alphabet, both networks
have the **same nodes** -- which is what `permutation_htna()` and
`plot_htna_diff()` compare edge by edge.

## Plotting per cohort

`plot_htna()` iterates over cohorts and draws one network per element.
It does not manage the layout grid -- wrap with `par(mfrow = ...)` if
you want a panel:

```{r, fig.height = 5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot_htna(grp)
par(op)
```

## Per-actor sequences per cohort

`sequence_plot_htna()` works the same way:

```{r, fig.height = 8}
sequence_plot_htna(grp,   type = "index")
```

## Centralities per cohort

`centralities_htna(grp)` returns one tidy data frame, with a leading
`group` column identifying the cohort:

```{r}
ct <- centralities_htna(grp)
head(ct, 10)
```

`plot_centralities()` draws one panel per measure and overlays one
line-and-point profile per cohort, so cohort-level differences on each
measure read along the same node axis:

```{r, fig.height = 9}
plot_centralities(grp, by = "group")
```

## Bootstrap per cohort

`bootstrap_htna(grp)` runs the bootstrap on each cohort and returns
a group of bootstrap results. `plot_htna_bootstrap()` iterates again:

```{r, fig.height = 5}
boots <- bootstrap_htna(grp, iter = 200)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot_htna_bootstrap(boots, display = "significant")
par(op)
```

## Centrality stability per cohort

`centrality_stability_htna(grp)` runs the case-dropping centrality
stability check on each cohort and returns a named list of
`htna_stability` objects. Each cohort's `cs` reports the largest
session-drop proportion at which `InStrength`, `OutStrength`, and
`Betweenness` still correlate with the originals at the default
0.7 / 0.95 threshold:

```{r}
stab <- centrality_stability_htna(grp, iter = 100, seed = 1)
stab
```

The report lists the CS-coefficient of each measure within each cohort.
By the Epskamp et al. (2018) convention, CS > 0.25 is acceptable and
CS > 0.5 is preferred for inferential use; the maximum reportable
value is the upper bound of the drop-proportion grid. A cohort
comparison of centralities is only meaningful for measures that are
stable in *both* cohorts.

## Comparing the two cohorts

Both networks share an alphabet, so their edges can be compared one by
one. Pass the grouped network as it is to `permutation_htna()`: it tests
every cohort pair and returns one result per pair, named
`"<first> vs <second>"`. `plot_htna_diff()` draws each pair as the
difference network *first minus second*, titled with the pair name;
positive differences are green, negative red, and only the edges that
differ significantly are drawn:

```{r}
perm <- permutation_htna(grp, iter = 500, seed = 1)
plot_htna_diff(perm)
```

With `show_nonsig = TRUE` the non-significant differences are added as
dashed grey edges, so the full difference network is visible together
with the significance verdict:

```{r}
plot_htna_diff(perm, show_nonsig = TRUE)
```

## Cohort-level pattern comparison

`permutation_htna()` tests edge-level differences between cohorts.
For *pattern*-level differences — recurring k-grams that
characterise one cohort over the other — see the [sequence
comparison vignette](sequence-comparison.html). The same grouped
network feeds directly into `sequence_compare_htna()`, which also
supports a `level = "type"` option that runs the comparison on
meta-paths (e.g. `Human -> AI -> Human`) rather than concrete
state codes.

## Working with the grouped object

Pass the result of `build_htna(..., group = ...)` as it is to the
functions above; each one iterates over the cohorts (or, for
`permutation_htna()`, `bayes_compare_htna()` and `compare_htna()`, over
the cohort pairs) and labels its output with the cohort names. There is
no need to extract cohorts by hand. To analyse a single cohort on its
own, build it directly from that cohort's sessions, e.g.
`build_htna(subset(human_ai, phase == "Early"), actor_type = "actor_type")`,
which yields the same network as the `Early` element of `grp`.
